lines.en: You live right on top of a fault line. Every few years, the ground decides to dance.
So you build a normal building. When the quake hits, the ground yanks the bottom, but the top wants to stay put.
It whips back and forth, until the columns snap.
So this time, you drive long concrete piles all the way down to solid rock, so the building can't sink into the shaking mud.
On top, you pour one thick slab of concrete that ties them all together.
But here's the real trick. You don't attach the building to the ground at all.
You set it on giant rubber pads with lead cores. They bend sideways, so the ground moves, and the building barely does.
Around the base, you leave an empty gap, so the building has room to slide without slamming into anything.
Then you wrap every column's steel bars in tight rings, so they bend instead of exploding.
You add diagonal braces with shock absorbers that squeeze the shaking into heat.
And at the very top, you hang a giant steel ball. When the building sways one way, it swings the other, and calms everything down.
Now the ground starts dancing again. The pads stretch, the dampers squeeze, the ball swings, and the building just stands there.
Add windows, an elevator, and some neighbors. Congratulations! You have built an earthquake-proof building.
